unmergedDoubts.whyNotMerged: Merged after review, recorded here because the enforcement point genuinely differs: IH is a hard dispatch gate that refuses the line before it becomes a prompt; codex evaluates three orthogonal predicates at list-construction time (is_visible platform/build, side-conversation allowlist, during-task exhaustive match); grok advertises a per-session Copy snapshot whose Default is all-false and ships the live tool-name list out-of-band in ACP AvailableCommandsUpdate.meta, so a client ignoring _meta offers commands it cannot run. Same capability, three enforcement points.

dsh tool-presentation-mode-policy was explicitly NOT merged into screen-mode-policy despite the shared 'presentation mode' vocabulary. It selects the MODEL-FACING tool surface (native schemas vs run_code+SDK prompt vs both) with a scoped nearest-wins presentAs override; the others decide terminal rendering mode (alt-screen vs inline). Merging on the word 'presentation' would have been a name-driven false merge.

codex screen-mode-and-terminal-capability-detection is ONE inventory entry spanning two of my rows (alt-screen decision policy AND the TTY requirement + bounded 100 ms cursor/color/keyboard-enhancement probe). Hard rule 2 forbids citing one source mechanism twice, so I placed the whole entry in terminal-capability-detection (which the mechanism name itself names) and left the screen-mode-policy row codex-free. Same collision on codex app-server-notification-contract-and-capability-negotiation: it is both the wire-format contract (row: wire-event-envelope-and-acceptance) and a per-connection capability negotiation, and I placed it only in the former, which makes handshake-capability-negotiation codex-free even though codex genuinely negotiates capabilities. Codex's composite inventory entries under-represent it in two rows; a reader comparing row membership must know this.

Placed as a required single-member row, but flagged: render-export-seam is largely renderer-internal (chunked renderToAnsiString, StaticKeybindingProvider deliberately omitting ChordInterceptor because useInput would hang with no stdin, ansiToSvg/ansiToPng rasterization, screenshotClipboard) which the taxonomy marks OUT of scope. Only the seam itself is arguably backend interface - chunk size 40, the ceiling/empty-strip termination contract, and the requirement that a chunk seam must not break tool_use<->tool_result grouping. A reviewer may prefer to drop this row from the interface domain; I kept it because the brief forbids skipping mechanisms.

Both are 'the presentation layer configures the engine' but at different layers. dsh settings-seam is the consumer-facing service a configuration UI talks to (namespace registration, redacted describe(), path-addressed SettingsPathOp so a redacted view cannot rebuild a section and delete secrets, SETTINGS_CONFLICT with expected/actual revisions). codex operator-config-layer-stack is engine-side config RESOLUTION (multi-source layer stack, requirements constraining lower layers, managed-features path, source attribution, permission-profile catalog). Collapsing a consumption seam into a resolution model was not justifiable.

Merged as subscriber-routing-and-bounded-replay, but this is the weakest merge in the domain and the row should be read as a family. dsh is a typesafe allowlisted forward contract ($on, 19 allowlisted events, two waterfall entries) whose consumer face omits an augmentation and fails to compile rather than no-op; codex is a renderer-side bounded ring buffer (32768 events/thread, 4 KiB coalesce cap, 256 KiB budget, front-first eviction) with thread-id classification and a narrow rebase allowlist. What they share is only 'how a subscriber is fed'.

Kept as two rows although both live on the same stdio stream. sdk-control-protocol is the wire protocol (21 request subtypes, request_id correlation, separate stdout/stdin envelope unions, error responses re-stating pending_permission_requests). structured-io-transport is the process-level carrier (NDJSON line-splitting, a single stdout writer so a control_request cannot overtake queued stream_events, abort resolving locally without host ack, resolvedToolUseIds duplicate suppression). Protocol and transport, not one capability.

Both hand a renderer derived state as a wholesale snapshot rather than incremental patches, and both care about the running row being carried out-of-band. But grok's is one typed per-session broadcast with a golden-JSON wire test and a required sessionId routing key; dsh's is a registry of versioned projection units (sessionStats v1, tokenUsage v2, contextPressure/contextBreakdown v4) where a missing key means capability-absence, never zero. The shared idea did not survive close reading.

A tempting single 'host capability detection' family that I deliberately did not form. dsh's probeReport surface is described only inside its screen-mode mechanism and has no standalone inventory entry in any source, so it is unreferenceable as a member; cc-custom headless-stdin-override is a stream substitution that merely requires TTY facts (with CI / mcp argv / win32 opt-outs); cc-custom terminal-capability-detection is a static env allowlist computed once at module load. Grouping them would have required inventing member names, which the brief forbids.

Placing opencode-upstream and opencode-fork members in the SAME row is deliberate, not an oversight: the fork's own evidence (packages/core/src/public-event-manifest.ts re-exporting EventManifest.ServerDefinitions; opencode/src/event-manifest.ts re-exporting Definitions/Durable/Latest from the schema package) shows the fork inherits the upstream mechanism rather than designing a different one. Treating upstream and fork as two independent sources here would have manufactured a false disagreement.
